evals.prompt: I run the affiliate program at Thrivelane, a B2B project-ops SaaS. 410 active partners, 20% recurring commission capped at 12 months, about $95K/month going out in commissions. Our network's built-in dashboard already gives us clicks, signups, EPC and total commissions earned, and I just paste that into a slide every month. Our CFO keeps asking whether the program actually makes money and I've got nothing solid. Put together what our affiliate dashboard should actually measure.
evals.expected_output: A dashboard specification document for a B2B recurring revenue-share program: billing spine as source of truth with the network export demoted to clicks only, validated-not-gross reporting, the four floor metrics, cost of sale with all fees inside the numerator, and EPC deleted from the B2B set.
expectations: Delivers a dashboard specification document rather than instructions for building the dashboard inside a BI tool.
Rejects the affiliate platform's own export as the source of truth on the grounds that those are the claimant's numbers.
Keeps the affiliate platform as the source for clicks and traffic only, reconciled to the money spine.
Names the billing/orders spine as the default data foundation and gives its cost as roughly a day or two of reconciliation followed by near-zero standing cost.
Includes all four floor metrics: net program contribution, cost of sale, top-N partner concentration, and partner-sourced MRR/ARR.
Defines cost of sale with network fees, agency fees, and placement/tenancy fees inside the numerator, not commission alone.
Headlines validated or approved commission and shows pending separately, rather than headlining gross commission.
Excludes EPC from the metric set and gives recurring commission accruing over a conversion lag as the reason.
Defines net program contribution as attributed net revenue minus validated commission plus network, agency and placement fees.
Normalizes partner-sourced MRR/ARR by billing interval, dividing annual by 12 and quarterly by 3.
Gives every metric a one-sentence definition naming numerator, denominator, window, timezone, and counting method.
Records in the spec header which data foundation was chosen and what moved it there.

evals.prompt: Petalgrove is a DTC houseplant store, about 900 affiliates, 10% CPA on order value, 30-day cookie, last click. Coupon and cashback sites are the top six lines on our leaderboard every single month and our content partners look useless next to them. Leadership wants to cut the content budget and pay the coupon sites more. Tell me what to measure so I can settle this.
evals.expected_output: A metric and instrument plan that refuses the budget shift on last-click evidence, starts at the new-to-file screen, ranks the incrementality instruments by efficiency, and routes the resulting decisions to the right owners.
expectations: Names new-to-file share sliced by partner type as the first instrument to run, because it is the cheapest rung of the incrementality instruments.
States explicitly that new-to-file proves the customer was not already a customer, never that the partner caused the purchase.
Ranks the incrementality instruments as new-to-file screen, then commission-reduction test, then geo-lift test, then holdout test, and states the ranking out loud.
Notes value and effort run in the same order across those four instruments, so the right pick is the weakest instrument that still settles the live question.
Flags the commission-reduction test as carrying the highest compliance cost because it unilaterally changes a partner's economics.
Directs the user to the notice and rate-change clauses in the program terms before running a commission-reduction test.
Names the holdout test as the option the efficiency order starves and states the condition that promotes it anyway.
Adds a checkout-adjacent revenue share metric covering coupon, cashback and browser-extension revenue as a share of program revenue.
Declines to endorse shifting budget from content partners to coupon and cashback partners on last-click numbers alone.
States that last-click-only program ROI systematically inflates checkout-adjacent partners and starves content partners.
Routes low incrementality to a repricing decision and attribution manipulation to the fraud rule set, stating the dashboard surfaces the signal but decides neither.
Labels the ROI tile with its attribution basis, naming last-click and the 30-day cookie window.

evals.prompt: Quick one. I'm setting the target column on our affiliate dashboard for next year. Numbers I've got: our attributed ROAS is 14:1 and the network average I keep seeing quoted is 12:1. Our active-affiliate rate is 22%, and the typical published range is 10-30%. Top 10% of our affiliates drive 64% of revenue against the 71% figure that gets quoted everywhere. Reversal rate 6%. Write the target for these four metrics and tell me how we're doing.
evals.expected_output: Targets derived from the program's own history, with every published figure tagged as calibration only, the active definition challenged, and no health verdict issued from benchmark comparison.
expectations: Refuses to adopt the 12:1 network-average ROAS as the program's target and labels it calibration only.
Notes that trade-body and network ROAS figures come from parties with an incentive to inflate the channel.
Derives every target from the program's own history rather than from any published figure.
Tags each published figure with its provenance: vendor, trade body, synthesis, or the program's own derived baseline.
Declines to read the 22% active-affiliate rate as healthy purely because it sits inside the published 10-30% range.
Flags the active-affiliate rate as uninterpretable until the program declares what counts as active and over what window.
Requires the active definition to be a meaningful action such as a validated conversion or live placement inside a fixed window, not a signup or a lone click.
Notes the top-10%-drives-71% figure has no published raw data behind it and declines to set it as a target.
Bands the 6% reversal rate against the program's own derived history rather than only against the published quality-problem line near 10%.
States the 14:1 figure is unreproducible without its attribution basis and its denominator stated.
Distinguishes attributed ROAS from attributed ROI and asks whether COGS sits in the denominator before treating 14:1 as either.
Does not declare the program healthy or unhealthy on the strength of the benchmark comparisons alone.

evals.prompt: Board deck is Thursday. Our CRM says partner-sourced ARR is $2.1M and partner-influenced ARR is $3.4M for the year. I want one big partner-attributed ARR tile showing $5.5M, plus whatever else you think belongs next to it on the exec view. B2B SaaS, around 250 partners, mostly agencies and consultancies.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to produce the combined tile, two separate capped numbers with a stated precedence rule, and an executive view carrying contribution and concentration.
expectations: Refuses to produce the combined $5.5M partner-attributed ARR tile.
Reports partner-sourced and partner-influenced ARR as two separate, capped numbers.
States that a deal qualifying as both sourced and influenced counts as sourced only.
Describes influenced revenue as a directional advocacy metric rather than bookable channel revenue.
Keeps influenced revenue in its own tile and outside any revenue total.
Names double-counted partner revenue as the consequence of summing the two numbers.
Places net program contribution on the executive view.
Places top-partner concentration on the same executive view.
Notes the influenced number costs roughly a quarter because a CRM influence model must exist and the precedence rule has to survive a political argument.
Ranks the influenced-revenue split low on efficiency because it changes how partner contribution is argued to an executive and nothing operational.
Gives every executive tile a value plus a delta against a stated prior period rather than a bare absolute number.
States the decision each executive tile informs.

evals.prompt: Our affiliate dashboard has exactly one alert: an email to the whole team if daily program revenue drops below $10,000. It fires constantly in January and never in Q4, so everyone filters it into a folder nobody opens. We're B2C, around 1,200 affiliates, and we do pay a handful of PPC partners. Redesign the alerting for us: what should fire, and at what number.
evals.expected_output: An alert register built on rolling-baseline thresholds, each with owner, channel and expected response time, shipped in the stated efficiency order with the brand-bidding flag promoted for the PPC partners.
expectations: Replaces the static $10,000 floor with a rolling-baseline dynamic threshold.
Gives a concrete rolling-baseline rule, such as deviation beyond 2 standard deviations from a 30-day rolling mean.
Attaches four fields to every alert: threshold, owner, delivery channel, and expected response time.
States that a threshold with no owner is decoration.
Ships the alerts in the order reversal-rate spike, single-partner share spike, click-to-conversion anomaly, EPC drop, brand-bidding flag, and states that ordering out loud.
Explains reversal-rate spike leads because it fires on money already at risk and reads off a state the platform already maintains.
Names the brand-bidding or trademark flag as the alert the efficiency order starves.
Promotes the brand-bidding flag anyway because this program pays PPC partners.
Advises stopping when the team's attention runs out rather than filling the alert strip.
Notes that the click-to-conversion anomaly and the EPC drop are one rolling-baseline rule over two numerators, so building either makes the second a copy.
States that fraud rule definitions and enforcement belong to the fraud rule set while the dashboard only surfaces the signals.
Recommends keeping an alert log recording fired, acknowledged by, and resolved in.

evals.prompt: We're building one affiliate dashboard for the whole company: our CMO, me (I run the program day to day), and two affiliate managers. Plan is a single live-refreshing screen everyone opens, same tiles for everyone, plus a separate fraud tool the managers check weekly. B2C ecommerce, 30-day cookie, 45-day validation window. Does that work? Lay out what it should look like.
evals.expected_output: Two audience views differing in metrics, a four-band cadence with named review rituals, fraud signals folded onto the operator view, and tiles carrying deltas against a stated prior period.
expectations: Rejects one refresh rate for the whole dashboard and calls it a defect.
Specifies four cadence bands: continuous or daily operational, weekly acquisition, monthly performance, and quarterly portfolio.
Assigns each band its own metrics and its own named review ritual stating who looks, in which meeting, deciding what.
States the four cadence bands carry no efficiency ranking and that all four get built.
Splits the dashboard into an executive view and an operator view.
States the two views differ in which metrics they carry, not only in level of detail.
Places fraud and compliance signals on the operator view rather than in a separate tool.
Gives the reason that daily decision-makers need performance and compliance signals at once.
Uses the layout convention KPI tiles, then trend or composition charts, then leaderboard or detail table, then alert strip.
Requires every tile to carry a value plus a delta against a stated prior period.
Puts net program contribution, cost of sale, new-to-file and top-partner share on the executive view.
Puts reversal rate, pending versus approved, single-partner share and conversion rate on the operator view.

evals.prompt: Ravencourt Outdoors, ecommerce affiliate program. One affiliate is 38% of our validated revenue and the top five together are 61%. I want to cap that partner's commission so the rest of the base catches up, and I need to know which concentration tiles to build. Also: three of our partners are actually sub-networks with hundreds of publishers underneath and they show as one row each. Should I split them into individual affiliates so the numbers look less scary?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to throttle the top partner, a concentration view at top-1/5/10% plus absolute top-5 share on the executive view, sub-networks counted as single credited entities, and the average-per-partner metric rejected.
expectations: Advises against capping or throttling the top partner's commission.
Prescribes partner development in the next tier down plus top-partner retention work as the response to a concentration breach.
Confirms that top five partners above 50% of revenue is a concentration problem.
Specifies top-1%, top-5% and top-10% shares plus the absolute top-5-partner share.
Computes the shares over active partners, using the spec's own active definition for the denominator population.
Places top-partner share on the executive view and reviews it quarterly.
States the concentration figures must be recomputed on the same definitions each quarter for the trend to be real.
Rejects splitting the sub-networks into their member publishers.
Counts each sub-network as one credited entity per conversion, with its own mix breakdown.
States that counting a sub-network's members as many partners distorts both partner counts and concentration.
Rejects average commission per active partner as a metric because the mean hides the skew that matters.
Offers top-decile share plus the median in place of the average.

evals.prompt: Need a sanity check before I send this. We lengthened our validation window from 30 days to 60 days at the start of March. Q2 cost of sale came in at 11.4% against 15.1% in Q1, and August alone is at 9.2%, which would be our best month ever. I want to headline that improvement on the dashboard and set 10% as the standing target. B2C, around 700 affiliates, return window is 30 days.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to compare the two periods or to headline the improvement, an immature-period flag on August, chart annotation requirements, and the comparability contract named as the fix.
expectations: Refuses to compare Q1 with Q2 because the two periods ran different validation windows.
Explains that reversal lag makes the more recent period look artificially good.
Flags August as an immature period whose validation window has not fully elapsed.
States a period is comparable only after its validation window fully elapses.
Declines to set 10% as a standing cost-of-sale target on the strength of these figures.
Requires validation-window changes to be annotated on every chart.
Requires program-term changes to be annotated on charts as well.
Keeps pending and approved conversions as separate states rather than mixing them into one total.
Names the comparability contract, covering event definition, date basis, timezone, currency and counting method, as what fixes the state per metric.
States the comparability contract must be fixed before any metric is specified, because changing it later invalidates all history.
Confirms the cost-of-sale numerator includes network, agency and placement fees before any figure is trusted.
Does not present the cost-of-sale drop as a genuine improvement or trend.

evals.prompt: Situation: Halden Freight Software, B2B SaaS, affiliate program is 14 months old with 180 partners. I have no analyst, it's me and a spreadsheet. Board meeting is in three weeks and I need something in front of them by then. Our affiliate platform exports conversions and commissions; the partner ID never makes it into our billing system or our CRM, and we have no warehouse. What goes on the dashboard?
evals.expected_output: A spine-pinned minimal spec, with every metric the constraints rule out deleted outright into Open items alongside what would make it computable, and the interview answers named as what moved each option.
expectations: Asks the three re-ranking questions, covering the date the first version must land, one-off win versus compounding asset, and the effort ceiling, before proposing metrics.
Asks clarifying questions one per message rather than delivering the whole questionnaire in a single block.
Pins the spec to the billing or orders spine because of the near date.
Deletes the modeled warehouse outright rather than listing it lower in the spec.
Deletes the brand-bidding alert and the creative slice outright given the thin effort ceiling.
Deletes new-to-file share from the spec because the partner ID does not reach billing or CRM.
Deletes churn-adjusted partner LTV, noting the program is not old enough for a 24-month horizon.
Lists every deleted metric, dimension and alert under Open items.
States for each deleted item what would make it computable.
Names stamping the partner ID at order or account creation as the prerequisite for new-to-file and for sourced-versus-influenced.
States the customer-file join costs roughly a month or two of work.
Names partner-sourced MRR/ARR as blocked by the missing partner ID in billing and records it under Open items rather than silently dropping it.

evals.prompt: My VP wants me to present the framework we're using for affiliate reporting. She likes named methodologies and she'll ask for one by name. Our current headline KPIs are total clicks (we target 1M/month), affiliate signups (200/month), and gross commissions earned. Give me the framework name and the KPI set to present.
evals.expected_output: A plain statement that no canonical affiliate-dashboard framework exists, the four borrowed pieces named and attributed, and the vanity KPIs demoted into a tiered metric set where every metric carries a named decision.
expectations: States plainly that no canonical affiliate-dashboard framework exists.
States that affiliate metric definitions are not standardized and that no standards body enforces them.
Declines to invent, name, or present a branded framework.

Names the borrowed pieces instead: incrementality measurement, the attributed ROAS versus attributed ROI split, the sourced-versus-influenced separation rule, and a tiered metric hierarchy with good-metric criteria.
Attributes the tiered hierarchy and the good-metric criteria to Croll and Yoskovitz's Lean Analytics.
Lists the four good-metric criteria: comparative, a ratio or rate, understandable, and behavior-changing.
Demotes clicks and signups from headline KPIs to diagnostics.
Names clicks, impressions and signups as vanity metrics that inform no decision.
Replaces gross commissions earned with validated commission in the headline.
Requires every metric on the dashboard to carry a named decision it informs, and to be dropped otherwise.
Organizes the metric set into a business or headline tier, an input or driver tier, and a health or guardrail tier.
Labels any partner lifecycle chain such as recruit, activate, produce, grow as informal shorthand rather than a branded framework.

evals.prompt: Here is the metric list someone before me left on our affiliate dashboard, with no definitions at all: ROAS, ROI, AOV, conversion rate, EPC, active affiliate rate, new-to-file. B2C apparel, 30-day cookie, last click. Our orders database records returns, but tax and shipping are both sitting inside the revenue column. Write the definition for each one so that two people compute the same number.
evals.expected_output: One-sentence definitions per metric with numerator, denominator, window, timezone and counting method, ROAS and ROI kept distinct, and the click, returns and active conventions declared explicitly.
expectations: Gives ROAS as attributed revenue divided by media cost.
Gives ROI with COGS added to the denominator, distinct from ROAS.
States explicitly whether COGS sits in the denominator and warns against using ROAS and ROI interchangeably.
Specifies AOV net of returns and excluding tax and shipping, and states that convention in the definition.
States AOV decides nothing unless it is sliced by partner type.
Defines the conversion rate with unique clicks in the denominator and declares the click convention.
Notes that what counts as a click, whether raw, unique, deduplicated or bot-filtered, varies by source, which is why the convention must be stated.
Declares which EPC convention applies: per click, per 100 clicks, or per visitor.
Warns that a blended network EPC predicts no individual affiliate's EPC and must not be used to set a partner target.
Defines the active-affiliate rate with a required meaningful action and a fixed window, naming both.
Defines new-to-file as conversions from customers not previously in the customer file divided by total partner conversions.
Keeps every definition to one sentence naming numerator, denominator, window, timezone, and counting method.
